claim: rsCaMPARI is a genetically encoded calcium marker engineered from a reversibly switchable fluorescent protein.
source: We introduce rsCaMPARI, a genetically encoded calcium marker engineered from a reversibly switchable fluorescent protein that enables spatiotemporally precise marking, erasing, and remarking of active neuron populations under brief, user-defined time windows of light exposure.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: rsCaMPARI enables spatiotemporally precise marking, erasing, and remarking of active neuron populations under brief, user-defined time windows of light exposure.
source: We introduce rsCaMPARI, a genetically encoded calcium marker engineered from a reversibly switchable fluorescent protein that enables spatiotemporally precise marking, erasing, and remarking of active neuron populations under brief, user-defined time windows of light exposure.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: rsCaMPARI photoswitching kinetics are modulated by calcium concentration when illuminating with blue light.
source: rsCaMPARI photoswitching kinetics are modulated by calcium concentration when illuminating with blue light, and the fluorescence can be reset with violet light.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1c.

claim: rsCaMPARI fluorescence can be reset with violet light.
source: rsCaMPARI photoswitching kinetics are modulated by calcium concentration when illuminating with blue light, and the fluorescence can be reset with violet light.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 1d.

claim: rsCaMPARI can mark and remark active neuron populations in freely swimming zebrafish.
source: We demonstrate the utility of rsCaMPARI for marking and remarking active neuron populations in freely swimming zebrafish.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: Traditional methods for identifying active neuron ensembles rely on immediate early genes (IEGs) such as Egr1/Zif268, c-Fos, or Arc.
source: Traditional methods for identifying active neuron ensembles have relied on exploiting the cellular machinery that control expression of immediate early genes (IEGs) such as Egr1/Zif268, c-Fos, or Arc (Morgan et al., 1987; Cole et al., 1989; Sheng and Greenberg, 1990; Lyford et al., 1995; Kawashima et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IEG-based methods have poor temporal resolution, typically on the scale of tens of minutes to hours.
source: However, the temporal resolution of these methods is poor, typically on the scale of tens of minutes to hours, and they do not correlate well with electrical activity (Sallaz and Jourdan, 1993; Sheng et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IEG-based methods do not correlate well with electrical activity.
source: However, the temporal resolution of these methods is poor, typically on the scale of tens of minutes to hours, and they do not correlate well with electrical activity (Sallaz and Jourdan, 1993; Sheng et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Calcium follows electrical activity more quantitatively than IEGs.
source: Calcium is an important second messenger in cell signaling pathways and neuron activity (Grienberger and Konnerth, 2012), which follows electrical activity more quantitatively (Helmchen et al., 1997; Bajar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GCaMPs are single-wavelength calcium indicators that enable visualization of calcium transients with fast kinetics.
source: For example, GCaMPs (Tian et al., 2009; Akerboom et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013) are single-wavelength calcium indicators that have enabled the visualization of calcium transients with fast kinetics, but their requirement for constant monitoring limit the size of the field of view, and recording neural activity in freely moving specimens is challenging.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GCaMPs require constant monitoring which limits the size of the field of view.
source: For example, GCaMPs (Tian et al., 2009; Akerboom et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013) are single-wavelength calcium indicators that have enabled the visualization of calcium transients with fast kinetics, but their requirement for constant monitoring limit the size of the field of view, and recording neural activity in freely moving specimens is challenging.
evidence: This is a known limitation of GCaMPs discussed in the introduction.

claim: Recording neural activity with GCaMPs in freely moving specimens is challenging.
source: For example, GCaMPs (Tian et al., 2009; Akerboom et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013) are single-wavelength calcium indicators that have enabled the visualization of calcium transients with fast kinetics, but their requirement for constant monitoring limit the size of the field of view, and recording neural activity in freely moving specimens is challenging.
evidence: This is a known limitation of GCaMPs discussed in the introduction.

claim: CaMPARIs are photoconvertible calcium integrators that enable optical selection and post-hoc analysis of evoked calcium activity across large tissue volumes.
source: CaMPARIs (Fosque et al., 2015; Moeyaert et al., 2018) are photoconvertible calcium integrators that have enabled optical selection and post-hoc analysis of the evoked calcium activity across large tissue volumes during a specific epoch of interest.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Alternative approaches have coupled calcium activity with light activation to drive the activation of transcription factors.
source: Alternative approaches have coupled calcium activity with light activation in order to drive the activation of transcription factors (Lee et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One major limitation of calcium sensors that rely on photoconversion or light activation is their irreversibility.
source: One major limitation of calcium sensors that rely on photoconversion or light activation is their irreversibility, which is useful when a permanent signal is desired; however, this irreversibility also hinders reuse of the tool, especially when multiple snapshots of activity are desired from the same sample preparation.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the properties of photoconvertible sensors.

claim: Irreversibility of photoconvertible calcium sensors hinders reuse of the tool when multiple snapshots of activity are desired from the same sample preparation.
source: One major limitation of calcium sensors that rely on photoconversion or light activation is their irreversibility, which is useful when a permanent signal is desired; however, this irreversibility also hinders reuse of the tool, especially when multiple snapshots of activity are desired from the same sample preparation.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the properties of photoconvertible sensors.

claim: Multiple snapshots are desirable when comparing active neuron ensembles in non-stereotyped organisms where there is variability in neural circuitry across different individuals.
source: Multiple snapshots are desirable when comparing active neuron ensembles in non-stereotyped organisms where there is variability in neural circuitry across different individuals, or where there is variability from trial to trial in the same individual.
evidence: This is a logical inference about experimental design needs.

claim: Multiple snapshots are desirable when there is variability from trial to trial in the same individual.
source: Multiple snapshots are desirable when comparing active neuron ensembles in non-stereotyped organisms where there is variability in neural circuitry across different individuals, or where there is variability from trial to trial in the same individual.
evidence: This is a logical inference about experimental design needs.

claim: An erasable calcium marker would enable multiple snapshots of neuronal activity to be captured quickly within the same sample preparation.
source: Such an erasable calcium marker would enable multiple snapshots of neuronal activity to be captured quickly within the same sample preparation.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the utility of an erasable marker.

claim: Reversibly switchable fluorescent proteins can be toggled between a fluorescent state (on) and a non-fluorescent state (off) depending on the wavelength of light used for illumination.
source: These proteins can be toggled between a fluorescent state (on) and a non-fluorescent state (off) depending on the wavelength of light used for illumination (Zhou and Lin, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Dronpa is a bright green fluorescent protein that can be off-switched with blue light illumination.
source: For example, Dronpa (Ando et al., 2004), rsEGFP (Grotjohann et al., 2011), and mGeos (Chang et al., 2012) are bright green fluorescent proteins that can be off-switched with blue light illumination.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: rsEGFP is a bright green fluorescent protein that can be off-switched with blue light illumination.

claim: mGeos is a bright green fluorescent protein that can be off-switched with blue light illumination.

source: Subsequent illumination with violet light reverts them back to the on-state.

claim: The structural mechanism underlying reversible switching behavior is a cis/trans isomerization of the chromophore, which is coupled to the chromophore's protonation state.
source: The structural mechanism underlying this reversible switching behavior is a cis/trans isomerization of the chromophore, which is coupled to the chromophore's protonation state (Andresen et al., 2005; Andresen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: rsCaMPARI was engineered such that the photoswitching kinetics are Ca2+-dependent.
source: Using directed evolution methods, we engineered the off-switching kinetics of rsCaMPARI under blue light illumination to be Ca2+-dependent, which allows reversible calcium activity marking with cellular resolution.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section.

claim: rsCaMPARI allows reversible calcium activity marking with cellular resolution.
source: Using directed evolution methods, we engineered the off-switching kinetics of rsCaMPARI under blue light illumination to be Ca2+-dependent, which allows reversible calcium activity marking with cellular resolution.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section.

claim: rsCaMPARI enables erasable and repeatable calcium activity marking over practical timescales of a few seconds.
source: The fluorescence can be easily recovered with violet light for immediate reuse and enables erasable and repeatable calcium activity marking over practical timescales of a few seconds.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section.

claim: rsCaMPARI can mark, erase, and re-mark cells with elevated calcium in primary neuron cultures.
source: We demonstrate the utility of rsCaMPARI for marking, erasing, and re-marking cells with elevated calcium in primary neuron cultures and freely swimming zebrafish.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: rsCaMPARI exhibited ~17 fold faster off-switching kinetics in high calcium compared to low calcium during illumination with blue marking light.
source: During illumination with blue 'marking light' (470–490 nm, 200 mW/cm2, Figure 1—figure supplement 8e), rsCaMPARI exhibited ~17 fold faster off-switching kinetics in high calcium compared to low calcium (Figure 1c) and the off-switching rate was linear with respect to the light power (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1c with quantitative data.

claim: The off-switching rate of rsCaMPARI was linear with respect to the light power.
source: During illumination with blue 'marking light' (470–490 nm, 200 mW/cm2, Figure 1—figure supplement 8e), rsCaMPARI exhibited ~17 fold faster off-switching kinetics in high calcium compared to low calcium (Figure 1c) and the off-switching rate was linear with respect to the light power (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: The recovery of rsCaMPARI fluorescence back to the bright on-state was very efficient when exposed to violet erasing light.
source: When exposed to violet 'erasing light' (390–410 nm, 200 mW/cm2), the recovery of rsCaMPARI fluorescence back to the bright on-state was very efficient and had similar on-switching kinetics in either high- or low-calcium conditions (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1d.

claim: rsCaMPARI had similar on-switching kinetics in either high- or low-calcium conditions.
source: When exposed to violet 'erasing light' (390–410 nm, 200 mW/cm2), the recovery of rsCaMPARI fluorescence back to the bright on-state was very efficient and had similar on-switching kinetics in either high- or low-calcium conditions (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The calcium-free state of rsCaMPARI was ~2-fold brighter than the calcium-bound state.
source: Measurement of green fluorescence intensity as a function of free calcium concentration showed that the calcium-free state was ~2-fold brighter than the calcium-bound state (Figure 1e,f), and indicated an apparent dissociation constant of 167 ± 6 nM (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1e,f with quantitative data.

claim: rsCaMPARI has an apparent dissociation constant of 167 ± 6 nM based on fluorescence intensity measurements.
source: Measurement of green fluorescence intensity as a function of free calcium concentration showed that the calcium-free state was ~2-fold brighter than the calcium-bound state (Figure 1e,f), and indicated an apparent dissociation constant of 167 ± 6 nM (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1f with quantitative data.

claim: Measurement of the off-switching rate vs. free calcium concentration gave an apparent dissociation constant of 181 ± 11 nM.
source: Measurement of the off-switching rate vs. free calcium concentration gave a similar apparent dissociation constant of 181 ± 11 nM (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1f with quantitative data.

claim: The calcium affinity of rsCaMPARI is similar to previously described CaMPARIs.
source: The calcium affinity of rsCaMPARI is therefore similar to previously described CaMPARIs (Fosque et al., 2015; Moeyaert et al., 2018) and GCaMPs (Tian et al., 2009; Akerboom et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013), suggesting that the dynamic range of rsCaMPARI calcium sensitivity falls within the physiological range of neuronal calcium transients.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cited literature.

claim: The calcium affinity of rsCaMPARI is similar to GCaMPs.
source: The calcium affinity of rsCaMPARI is therefore similar to previously described CaMPARIs (Fosque et al., 2015; Moeyaert et al., 2018) and GCaMPs (Tian et al., 2009; Akerboom et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013), suggesting that the dynamic range of rsCaMPARI calcium sensitivity falls within the physiological range of neuronal calcium transients.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cited literature.

claim: Neurons illuminated with 10 s of marking light accompanied by field stimulation exhibited strong dimming of the green fluorescence signal.
source: Neurons illuminated with 10 s of marking light accompanied by field stimulation exhibited strong dimming of the green fluorescence signal (Figure 2a, cycle 1), which could later be recovered by a 3-s pulse of erasing light.

claim: rsCaMPARI fluorescence could be recovered by a 3-s pulse of erasing light.
source: Neurons illuminated with 10 s of marking light accompanied by field stimulation exhibited strong dimming of the green fluorescence signal (Figure 2a, cycle 1), which could later be recovered by a 3-s pulse of erasing light.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a.

claim: When the same neuron was subsequently illuminated with marking light but without field stimulation, only modest dimming of the green fluorescence was observed.
source: When the same neuron was subsequently illuminated with marking light but without field stimulation, only modest dimming of the green fluorescence was observed (Figure 2a, cycle 2).

claim: The same neuron could be repeatedly marked and erased over several cycles.
source: The same neuron could be repeatedly marked and erased over several cycles (Figure 2a, cycles 3–6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Non-stimulated neurons exhibited minimal photoswitching during marking light exposure.
source: While the non-stimulated neurons exhibited minimal photoswitching, we observed significantly more photoswitching in stimulated neurons and higher frequencies resulted in more photoswitching.

claim: Stimulated neurons exhibited significantly more photoswitching than non-stimulated neurons.

source: While the non-stimulated neurons exhibited minimal photoswitching, we observed significantly more photoswitching in stimulated neurons and higher frequencies resulted in more photoswitching.

claim: The broad variability observed in the marked signal is presumably due to the natural variability among neurons.
source: The broad variability we observed in the marked signal is presumably due to the natural variability among neurons and this variability was previously observed for GCaMP in similar neuron preparations (Wardill et al., 2013).

claim: The largest fluorescence change was observed during the first train of field stimulations.
source: In response to three trains of 160 action potentials during marking light, we observed the largest fluorescence change during the first train (~40–60% green fluorescence decrease compared to ~10% in non-stimulated neurons).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Smaller fluorescence changes were observed during the second and third field pulse trains as the sensor approached near complete off-switching.
source: Smaller fluorescence changes were observed during the second and third field pulse trains as the sensor approached near complete off-switching.

claim: rsCaMPARI green fluorescence is stable in the dark for more than 1 hr.
source: We tracked the fluorescence of neurons that had previously been illuminated with marking light and found that rsCaMPARI green fluorescence is stable in the dark for more than 1 hr (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), even during ongoing calcium activity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2d and supplementary figures.

claim: rsCaMPARI fluorescence is stable even during ongoing calcium activity.
source: We tracked the fluorescence of neurons that had previously been illuminated with marking light and found that rsCaMPARI green fluorescence is stable in the dark for more than 1 hr (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), even during ongoing calcium activity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2d and supplementary figures.

claim: rsCaMPARI is sufficiently stable for post-hoc analysis.
source: This provides sufficient time for readout of the recorded signal, for example with high-resolution microscopy techniques over large volumes of tissue, and demonstrates that rsCaMPARI is sufficiently stable for post-hoc analysis.

claim: rsCaMPARI lost ~50% of its initial fluorescence after 20 cycles of marking and erasing.

claim: More rapid off-switching of rsCaMPARI correlated well with action potential firing.

claim: Selective marking of the patched neuron could be repeated several times.

source: When the fish were anesthetized with the sodium channel blocker tricaine methanosulfonate (MS-222) to block brain activity during exposure to marking light, there was low and uniform labeling across the brain, consistent with a small amount of background photoswitching in the absence of calcium (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: In freely swimming zebrafish, neuron-specific labeling patterns were observed, particularly in the forebrain, habenula, and hindbrain.

claim: Reversibly switchable fluorescent proteins have not yet been exploited to create functional activity reporters prior to this work.

claim: The H62L mutant exhibited slow spontaneous recovery to the on-state with a half-time of several hours after photoswitching to the off-state.
